text: Welcome to session seventeen: autocorrelation, attributes and capability.
Today we fix charts for data that remember the past, chart defect counts, and ask whether CellCo's coating is good enough for a demanding customer.
Here is the plan.
First autocorrelated data, then p and c charts. After the break, process capability, a negotiation between supplier and customer, and workshop eight.
A beta gauge scans the web every second. Consecutive readings are close, because the oven, slurry and foil change slowly. The data are autocorrelated.
For CellCo's continuous readings, the lag-one autocorrelation is 0.7.
Standard charts assume independent points. With autocorrelation the moving range is small, so the limits come out at about plus or minus 1.64 process standard deviations instead of three.
About ten percent of in-control points then fall outside the limits. The remedy is to fit a time-series model and chart its residuals.
This chart shows three hundred readings from a process that is in control throughout. Every red point is a false alarm.
Move the autocorrelation slider. At zero, false alarms are rare. At 0.7, about one point in ten signals.
Now switch to the residuals of the time-series model. The false alarms almost disappear.
When we can only count, we use attribute charts.
A p chart tracks the fraction defective. For lots of five hundred cells with an average of 3.5 percent defective, the limits are 1.03 and 5.97 percent.
A c chart tracks defects per unit, such as pinholes per hundred square meters of electrode. With an average of four, the limits are zero and ten.
Attribute charts need far more data than charts of measurements. Measure where you can, and count where you cannot.
Let us take a ten-minute break.
Afterwards: the process is in control. Is it capable?
In control means stable and predictable. Capable means that the predictable output fits the specification.
C p compares the specification width with six sigma. For CellCo it is 1.16.
C p k also accounts for the mean being off center. It is 1.07, and about 770 parts per million fall outside the specification, almost all above the upper limit.
C p k uses the within-subgroup sigma; P p k uses the overall sigma, which includes drift. And all parts-per-million figures assume a normal distribution, so check the tails.
Move the mean and the standard deviation, or use the presets.
Re-centering at twenty cuts the out-of-specification rate by 37 percent, to about 485 parts per million, with no change in variation.
Reaching a C p k of 1.33 also requires sigma to fall to 0.150, thirteen percent below today.
Activity, a specification negotiation. Paired groups work for twenty-five minutes.
One group plays CellCo, the supplier. The other plays a storage integrator, the customer, who requires a C p k of 1.33.
CellCo can re-center the die for 0.1 million yuan, or buy a new slot die with closed-loop control for 1.2 million. Each hundred parts per million costs the customer 0.15 million yuan a year.
Agree a plan and who pays what. Each side may concede only with a number that supports it.
Here are the four combinations.
Only re-centering together with the new die meets a C p k of 1.33, at 63 parts per million.
That plan saves the customer 1.06 million yuan a year against doing nothing, so the 1.3 million investment pays back in about fifteen months. That saving is the customer's reason to share the cost.
Re-centering is the obvious first step at any price, and it also saves cathode material.
Workshop eight. Fit a time-series model to five hundred readings and chart the residuals, build a p chart for thirty lots, and compute capability and the variation reduction needed for 1.33.
Let us summarize.
Autocorrelated data make standard limits too narrow. Chart model residuals instead.
P and c charts monitor counts, but need more data than charts of measurements.
In control is not capable. CellCo is at a C p k of 1.07; re-centering plus a thirteen percent cut in sigma reaches 1.33.
